extracted.intended_audience: students learning introductory combinatorics / discrete mathematics (high school or early-college)
extracted.subtask_description: Introductory combinatorics: counting lists (permutations) and subsets (combinations), including multiplication principle, factorials, permutations, binomial coefficients, Pascal's triangle, and the binomial theorem. Focused on solving concrete counting problems and avoiding common pitfalls (double-counting).

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of a list and equality of lists
rubrics_metrics.description: A list is an ordered sequence of entries; for two lists to be equal they must have exactly the same entries in exactly the same order. Consequently, equal lists have the same length. The empty list () is the unique list of length zero.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: a byte is a length-eight list of 0's and 1's; (a,15) is a length-two list; (0,(0,1,1)) is a length-two list whose second entry is a list of length three. Anti-pattern: treating two lists with different orders as the same (order matters).

rubrics_metrics.name: Multiplication Principle (Fact 3.1)
rubrics_metrics.description: If making a list of length n has a1 choices for the first entry, a2 choices for the second, a3 for the third, and so on, then the total number of different lists is the product a1 * a2 * ... * an.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrated by a tree/diagram (Figure 3.1). Example: choosing a list with first entry in {a,b,c} (3 choices), second in {5,7} (2 choices), third in {a,x} (2 choices) gives 3*2*2=12 lists. Used throughout for license plates, phone numbers, etc.

rubrics_metrics.name: Repetition allowed vs repetition not allowed
rubrics_metrics.description: Distinguish two types of list-counting problems: repetition allowed (the same symbol may appear multiple times in different entries) and repetition not allowed (non-repetitive lists).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: license plates or telephone numbers allow repetition; drawing 5 cards from a standard deck and lining them up does not allow repetition. This distinction changes the counting: with repetition, use powers (e.g., 7^4); without repetition, use falling products (e.g., 7*6*5*4).

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoiding double-counting when partitioning by overlapping categories
rubrics_metrics.description: When dividing the desired objects into types/categories, ensure the categories are disjoint; otherwise lists can be counted multiple times.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anti-pattern illustrated: counting lists that 'contain at least one E' by summing counts for E in each position with repetition allowed leads to overcounting (a list like (E,E,A,B) belongs to multiple types). Correct approaches include complementary counting or constructing disjoint cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Factorial definition (Definition 3.1)
rubrics_metrics.description: For a non-negative integer n, n! (n factorial) is the number of non-repetitive lists of length n that can be made from n symbols. Thus 0! = 1, 1! = 1, and for n > 1, n! = n*(n-1)*(n-2)*...*2*1.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Properties and recurrence: n! = n*(n-1)!, examples: 2! = 2, 3! = 6, 4! = 24, etc. Explanation why 0! = 1 (consistency with recurrence and counting the empty list).

rubrics_metrics.name: Permutations / number of non-repetitive lists of length k from n symbols (Fact 3.2)
rubrics_metrics.description: The number of non-repetitive lists (ordered selections) of length k chosen from n symbols is n*(n-1)*(n-2)*...*(n-k+1), which can be written n!/(n-k)!.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: number of non-repetitive length-5 lists from 8 symbols is 8*7*6*5*4 = 8!/(8-5)! = 6720. Use multiplication principle to derive; convenient repackaging of repeated-multiplication idea.

rubrics_metrics.name: Binomial coefficient / 'n choose k' definition (Definition 3.2)
rubrics_metrics.description: (n choose k) denotes the number of k-element subsets that can be made by choosing k elements from an n-element set. If k < 0 or k > n then (n choose k) = 0.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: list of all k-element subsets of {a,b,c,d} for various k. Distinguish subsets (order does not matter) from lists (order matters).

rubrics_metrics.name: Formula for binomial coefficients (Fact 3.3)
rubrics_metrics.description: If n and k are integers with 0 <= k <= n, then (n choose k) = n! / (k! (n-k)!). Otherwise (n choose k) = 0.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Derivation: count k-permutations then divide by k! to account for the k! orderings of each k-element subset. Examples: (5 choose 3) = 10 computed via 5!/(3!2!).

rubrics_metrics.name: Counting by complement (use subtraction of complementary counts)
rubrics_metrics.description: To count objects with a condition 'at least one' (or similar), count the total and subtract the number of objects that fail the condition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: number of length-4 lists with repetition allowed that contain at least one E = total 7^4 minus number with no E (6^4) giving 2401 - 1296 = 1105. Also used to count lists with at least one repeated entry: total n^k minus number of non-repetitive lists.

rubrics_metrics.name: Counting by cases (partition into disjoint types)
rubrics_metrics.description: When a requirement can be split into disjoint scenarios (e.g., E occurs in position 1, 2, 3, or 4 with no overlap), count each case separately and sum.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example (no repetition): counting lists of length 4 that contain E by splitting into four types depending on position of E; each type yields 6*5*4 = 120, and summing four disjoint cases gives 480. Ensure cases are disjoint; otherwise combine with inclusion-exclusion or complementary counting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of tree/diagram representation for sequential choices
rubrics_metrics.description: Represent sequential choices using a branching diagram (tree); each path corresponds to a distinct list and counting paths yields the product of choices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Figure 3.1 demonstrates constructing lists of length 3 by branching first choice (3), second (2 each), third (2 each) to get 3*2*2 paths. Useful visual tool to justify multiplication principle.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pascal's identity and combinatorial proof (Equation 3.2)
rubrics_metrics.description: For integers n and k with 0 < k < n, (n+1 choose k) = (n choose k) + (n choose k-1). Combinatorial proof: count k-element subsets of an (n+1)-element set by splitting into those that contain a particular element (choose remaining k-1 from n) and those that do not (choose k from n).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This identity underlies Pascal's triangle construction and many combinatorial arguments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pascal's triangle and interpretation
rubrics_metrics.description: Arrange binomial coefficients in a triangular array with row n listing (n choose 0), (n choose 1), ..., (n choose n). Each interior entry equals the sum of the two numbers immediately above it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rows correspond to coefficients of (x+y)^n; can compute coefficients iteratively without factorial formula. Figure 3.2 and examples show correspondence with binomial coefficients.

rubrics_metrics.name: Binomial Theorem (Theorem 3.1)
rubrics_metrics.description: For non-negative integer n, (x + y)^n = sum_{k=0}^n (n choose k) x^{n-k} y^k, i.e., the coefficients of the expansion are binomial coefficients.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Connects algebraic expansion to combinatorial counting; examples of expansions for small n shown in Figure 3.3.

rubrics_metrics.name: Modeling applied counting problems by appropriate combinatorial objects
rubrics_metrics.description: Translate real-world counting tasks (license plates, telephone codes, card hands, lotteries) into lists, permutations, or subsets and apply the appropriate counting formula.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: standard license plate (3 letters then 4 numbers) -> length-7 list with 26*26*26*10*10*10*10 possibilities; 5-card poker hand -> 5-element subset of 52 cards giving (52 choose 5) = 2,598,960; lottery odds computed as (36 choose 6).
